title: Brand, web & creative production
summary: Taking an agency brand direction into production, building in Webflow, and bringing stalled tools through to launch.
intro: At Cryptonix, I worked across brand design, Webflow delivery, and creative operations. I helped turn an agency rebrand into a usable visual system and coordinated the people and technical details needed to ship websites, content, and tools.
metrics: pages launched by the team over roughly a year
public tools: invoices, receipts, and conversion

sections.title: Turn a rebrand into something the team can use
paragraphs: When I joined, Cryptonix used a dark identity with bright gradients. An agency rebrand was already underway, but extended approvals and changing scope left the handover incomplete. I maintained the existing brand, created social visuals, and worked on the website from design through Webflow implementation.

With a new marketing director, we revisited the agency material and I repeated the competitor review. We selected a white-and-orange direction and lightly adapted the proposed logo. The aim was to feel like familiar business infrastructure: clients wanted crypto payments, but the visual language needed to avoid the associations of speculative crypto culture.

sections.title: Give each team the assets it actually needs
paragraphs: I applied the direction across web, social media, sales, email, merchandise, and events. Illustrations shared colours and construction rules, making them useful to several teams. Social graphics used a consistent orange focal point and headline treatment.

Reuse differed by channel. I used the social templates myself; developers used the website system, marketing used email templates, and sales worked with presentation layouts. A shared library helped, but each handoff needed to fit the people and tools on the receiving end.

sections.title: Finish the last difficult part of a stalled tool
paragraphs: The crypto invoice generator had been stalled for about three months when I took it on. Most of the implementation was complete, but the remaining work involved cryptocurrency rounding, decimal precision, and API behaviour. The team lacked a shared understanding of how to resolve those details.

I decomposed the remaining tasks, separated responsibilities, and followed implementation through quality control. My experience in design and development, alongside an understanding of the product, helped bridge the gap between a nearly finished application and a working tool.

The wider tool work included a crypto receipt generator, a converter using current rates, and a separate partner-programme calculator. I coordinated design, development, and stakeholders for those projects. Getting them built also meant resolving different priorities around what marketing and sales needed.

sections.title: Make repeated delivery easier
paragraphs: For website production, I brought product facts, SEO requirements, and implementation constraints into briefs before design and development handoffs. Content work combined AI-assisted drafting with factual checks, proofreading, and editorial review.

Over roughly a year, the team launched more than 60 pages and the three public tools. The publishing workflow also increased output from about one article per month to around four. Coordination continued to require attention; the systems reduced ambiguity rather than removing every dependency.

Looking back, I would invest earlier in deeper content automation. At the time, much of my capacity went into approvals, agency handover, and keeping designers, developers, and content contributors aligned.

title: Performance creative at scale
summary: A practical layout system and specialist handoffs for high-volume regional campaigns.
role: Creative Director | Design Lead | Graphic Designer
intro: At Incentive Agency, I grew from hands-on designer into a creative director responsible for both campaign production and regional content. I built a small internal design team and a working system for adapting performance creatives across languages, formats, and client requirements.

sections.title: Let content drive the layout
paragraphs: Armenian headlines were a useful stress test: longer words made fixed templates and character limits unreliable. I borrowed ideas from responsive web design—minimum and maximum sizes, proportional relationships, and variables that influence surrounding elements.

The system connected type, spacing, and product placement so designers could adapt an offer across very narrow, tall, or compact placements. Regional managers also had different approval preferences, so the layouts needed room for practical adjustments.

images.name: recovered-apple-typography.webp
images.caption: Different word lengths required flexible relationships between the headline and supporting content.
images.alt: Different word lengths required flexible relationships between the headline and supporting content.

sections.title: Build a manual system people can operate
paragraphs: A designer took the offer text from a task and placed it into shared components, which carried the content into the format templates. They checked those layouts before handing the package to motion. The motion designer applied presets and adjusted the details where needed.

This was a manual production system. People still needed to recognize awkward combinations, incorrect information, and format-specific problems. Shared components and recurring treatments gave junior designers a workable starting point without pretending that every asset would be correct automatically.

sections.title: Put acceptance checks inside the handoffs
paragraphs: I hired two junior designers, replaced one as the workload changed, and later brought in a motion designer. As my content responsibilities expanded, I also delegated planning and deadline tracking to a social media manager. The team structure evolved with the actual workload.

The PPC owner could not inspect every package. Acceptance criteria between specialists handled routine checks: motion reviewed incoming graphics, and graphic designers reviewed the animation. Some client revisions came from incorrectly communicated offer terms, so internal design review could not prevent every change.

sections.title: Maintain the system under real workload
paragraphs: Production covered multiple regional markets and other agency clients. The exact market count varied, so the useful story is how the system handled more assets, languages, and people reviewing the work.

I kept track of capacity, holidays, promotion peaks, and changing client requirements. Task tracking, postmortems, acceptance criteria, and regular library maintenance helped keep the operation usable. It still depended on active management.
Today, I would automate more of the repeatable adaptation logic. That is a lesson from this project; the system I delivered relied on components, instructions, and specialist judgement.

coverAlt: Apple product imagery from the archived reseller portfolio
challenge: Campaign production depended on an expensive outsourced specialist, while regional requests and content work were growing. Junior designers needed a system they could use reliably under tight deadlines.
contribution: I hired and onboarded junior designers and a motion specialist, defined the design rules and acceptance criteria, and maintained the production process. Client-facing account work initially sat with the account manager and PPC project owner.

title: Visual storytelling for B2B music
summary: An expressive visual language for a B2B music service, designed around the resources of a small team.
intro: Zvuk Business provides music for commercial spaces. I adapted inherited brand elements into a practical B2B communication system and created a visual narrative that could explain abstract ideas across industries.
metrics: website pages launched with product and marketing
presentations designed with the sales team

sections.title: Turn inherited assets into working rules
paragraphs: The parent brand supplied SB Sans Display, a logo, and a pictogram. I selected violet from the available colour directions, refined its tone, and built a broader palette. Type hierarchy, spacing, and layout were defined in relation to the body-text size.

The system had to work for a small team producing many different communications. Clear rules created a common foundation for website visuals, compact icons, social posts, and enterprise presentations.

sections.title: Give an invisible service a visual story
paragraphs: Illustration could show what a photograph could not: sound, atmosphere, and the relationship between music and a business setting. Characters and familiar objects made the message concrete, with exaggeration and humour providing room to explain abstract concepts.

A typical composition combined a character, an industry-specific background, and a rounded brand shape. The character represented a customer, employee, or business owner; the setting established the use case. That repeatable structure made each image recognizable without forcing every story into the same scene.

sections.title: Build a library, then tailor the story
paragraphs: Reusable character and scene elements reduced the need to draw every visual from scratch. The same library could support different industries, and colours could be adapted for client-specific presentation contexts.

Social graphics paired illustrations with a clear title and subtitle. A contrasting green accent and variations of the rounded brand shape kept the feed varied while retaining the violet-led identity.

sections.title: Carry the language into sales and web
paragraphs: Enterprise sales needed tailored presentations rather than one generic deck. Illustration gave those decks a flexible way to represent the prospect’s business context. Website visuals used the same vocabulary to explain the service and its applications.

Across my work with the team, the visual toolkit supported more than 40 website pages and over 200 presentations. Reusable elements let us tailor the work to different clients while retaining a consistent visual language.

challenge: Music for a business is an invisible product. The brand needed to explain atmosphere, customer experience, and industry-specific use cases without falling back on generic personal-listening imagery.

title: Art direction & regional content
summary: Building regional creator production from initial experiments into an ongoing content programme.
role: Creative Director | Design Lead | Graphic Designer
intro: Incentive Agency had demonstrated creator content to a client, but needed a way to produce it repeatedly across regional accounts. I owned content strategy, concepts, art direction, budgets, and production coordination, working with local creators and account managers.
metrics: publications created from the programme’s output

sections.title: Build production beyond the first experiments
paragraphs: The agency had run initial shoots with creators in Ukraine and sold the service, but a repeatable production approach still needed to be built. I found creators through personal contacts, referrals, and social platforms, then onboarded and coordinated them through real assignments.

Early assignments were usually lower-priority briefs. I assessed the same qualities needed for ongoing work: quality, delivery speed, clear communication, and realistic capacity. A reliable creator raised risks early and avoided taking on more than they could complete.

sections.title: Plan around access, language, and availability
paragraphs: Creators rarely owned the newest devices. Product shoots often depended on a partner flagship store lending equipment, with paperwork and availability to arrange. Sometimes a suitable device owner in another region provided an alternative.

Casting also needed the right language and local context. Those requirements could overlap: a brief might need both device access and a suitable speaker. Location was one part of the decision, alongside availability, capability, and the regional budget.

sections.title: Stay close enough to resolve production problems
paragraphs: I stayed available during filming. Missing audio, an unexpected language mismatch, or a store unable to release equipment could put the brief at risk. Resolving those problems was part of production coordination, alongside protecting relationships with creators through client revisions.

Responsibilities were allocated to manage dependency as well as cost. Creators often edited their own work; when their filming workload grew, editing could move to a motion designer. I also filled gaps with my own filming when necessary. Different briefs needed different arrangements.

sections.title: Make the plan fit the budget
paragraphs: I worked with regional content plans and budgets, adjusting the mix of shoots, creator locations, and editing. Combining production where possible helped create more publishable material, but reuse across markets was uncommon and usually required re-editing.

The programme produced more than 800 publications from the material created. This is a count of published content items, rather than a count of separate shoots or videos. My responsibility was to keep the creative output moving while managing the people, costs, and practical constraints behind it.

challenge: Moving beyond a few initial shoots meant organizing device access, language requirements, creator capacity, and regional budgets. Production mistakes and unplanned revisions could quickly consume the agency’s margin.
contribution: I planned content, wrote and directed briefs, sourced and onboarded creators, coordinated equipment and filming, and controlled quality and spending. Local creators often handled locations and casting; editing stayed with the creator or moved to a motion designer when needed.

title: Modular sales collateral
summary: Clarifying a crypto-payments product and building editable presentation, one-pager, and proposal templates for sales.
role: Designer and strategist, collaborating with the Sales Lead
intro: A newly staffed Cryptonix sales team needed materials quickly and wanted to reshape them without a designer. I built the content structure with the Sales Lead, designed the toolkit, and assembled editable templates in Google Slides.

sections.title: Start with how the product is used
paragraphs: Through my work with the product, I had come to see two main ways of using it: integrating through the API, or operating through the dashboard. Existing marketing descriptions focused on plugins, buttons, and checkout pages, which could obscure that simpler distinction.
I organized the material around those two paths. The Sales Lead supplied knowledge of prospects and their use cases, helping us decide which capabilities mattered in each conversation.

 A[Shared product explanation] --> B[API integration]
 A --> C[Dashboard use]
 B --> D[Relevant workflows and capabilities]
 C --> D
 D --> E[Industry context]
 E --> F[Commercial proposal]
diagram.caption: The integration path establishes the context; relevant capabilities and commercial details complete the pitch.

summary.text: Start with a consistent account of what the service does.

summary.title: Choose the usage path
summary.text: API integration or day-to-day dashboard use.

summary.title: Select relevant capabilities
summary.text: Show what matters to this prospect, such as receiving payments or making payouts.

summary.title: Complete the proposal
summary.text: Adapt the industry examples and commercial material.

sections.title: Include the capabilities a prospect needs
paragraphs: A prospect needing mass payouts has a different conversation from one simply receiving payments. Some businesses need on/off-ramp capabilities; others already have payment providers and care most about fitting another service into their existing setup.

Working with sales, I adapted the content and slide variations around those needs. The toolkit covered presentations, one-pagers, and commercial proposals, with icons, cards, illustrations, and covers supporting the narrative.

sections.title: Make the toolkit easy to edit
paragraphs: I designed at 1920 × 1080 to make transferring elements from Figma straightforward, and kept elements native to Google Slides where practical. Placeholders let the sales team replace information in familiar template layouts.

The grid supported elements spanning different widths, and the components gave editors consistent options for content. The goal was a usable working package: sales could change a pitch without rebuilding its visual structure.

sections.title: Hand over work the team can use
paragraphs: After delivery, the team continued using the package and rarely returned for additions. That practical independence is the clearest result I observed.

I asked for feedback to guide improvements, but did not receive detailed responses. The case therefore focuses on the delivered toolkit and its continued use, without attributing sales performance to the presentation design.

challenge: Sales needed to start pitching with an incomplete set of materials. The product story mixed several features and integrations, making it harder to explain what a particular prospect would actually use.
contribution: I developed the narrative skeleton, refined it with the Sales Lead, designed the visual elements, and assembled the template system for the planned industry outreach.

title: Identity & website launch
summary: An identity, mascot, and Tilda website built for an influencer-matching service’s launch.
intro: In spring–summer 2023, I designed and built a Tilda website for an influencer-matching service initially targeting gaming businesses. The logo, mascot, and visual system supported that launch; the client team provided the name and copy.

sections.title: Build the identity around the launch
paragraphs: The project came through a former marketing director I had worked with at Zvuk. The client wanted an illustrated direction related to that work. Gaming was the initial business focus, which gave the character and visual tone a useful starting point.

I designed the wordmark and compact mark, then developed the typography, colour palette, and interface around the illustration. The identity supported a concrete deliverable: a website ready for campaign traffic.

sections.title: Give the gaming direction a character
paragraphs: Booster rides a vehicle somewhere between a space scooter and a rocket. The gaming context and the brand’s emphasis on success shaped the energetic character, with bold lettering and vivid colour following that direction.

The initial site included several illustrations, with a larger series envisaged. Later requirements reduced their role. When the site was adapted toward beauty businesses, we moved away from this illustrated language for that audience.

sections.title: Design for the way the site would be maintained
paragraphs: I used a triadic palette, clear text contrast, and a type-led spacing system. The main practical constraint was the Tilda implementation: I worked largely with standard blocks and design overrides to keep ongoing updates manageable.
That choice influenced the interface. Familiar section structures and reusable components gave the site a consistent foundation while keeping it close to the platform’s existing building blocks.

sections.title: Launch, then adapt to changing requirements
paragraphs: I designed and built the website from the team’s supplied copy. There was no dedicated user-behaviour analysis available, so I worked with familiar landing-page patterns and the client’s requirements.

The site launched, and I returned for two later rounds of updates, roughly a year and two years afterward. It continued under a different name with much of the design retained. The story is a delivered website and subsequent adaptations; conversion performance was not available to me.
